title: IPT versus antidepressants: individual participant data meta-analysis
fact: An individual participant data meta-analysis pooled 9 randomized trials (N = 1,536) comparing interpersonal psychotherapy with antidepressants in acute adult depression. Post-treatment depression severity and social functioning did not differ significantly between the two. Antidepressants did slightly better on a few secondary measures (general psychopathology, dysfunctional attitudes), and no differences were seen at follow-up.
source: Cohen ZD, Breunese J, Markowitz JC, et al. Comparative efficacy of interpersonal psychotherapy and antidepressant medication for adult depression: a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis. Psychological Medicine 2024;54(14):3785-3794.
note: Confirmed from abstract on experts.arizona.edu record (fetched); DOI as shown there.

title: NICE NG222 lists IPT as a first-line option
fact: The 2022 NICE depression guideline includes interpersonal therapy among the treatment options for both less severe and more severe new episodes of depression. For less severe depression it advises considering the least intrusive option first (guided self-help). IPT is also named for further-line treatment combined with medication.
source: NICE. Depression in adults: treatment and management. NG222. 2022.
note: Page fetched, but fetch summary did not show table cell text; IPT's presence in Tables 1 and 2 and recs 1.9.5, 1.11.2 reported by the fetch. Publication month not seen; recs marked [2022].

title: WHO Group Interpersonal Therapy (IPT-G) for depression manual
fact: WHO and Columbia University published an 84-page, 8-session group IPT manual (WHO/MSD/MER/16.4) as part of mhGAP. It is simplified for supervised facilitators without prior mental health training, and WHO describes IPT as a possible first-line depression treatment. It is available in 11 languages.
source: World Health Organization and Columbia University. Group Interpersonal Therapy (IPT) for Depression. Geneva: WHO; 2016 (WHO/MSD/MER/16.4).
note: WHO page fetched; it does not state whether the manual is current or superseded. Published 2016, so it is pre-2021 but is the manual itself; the PMC trial page (PMC7425581) was blocked, so no trial data cited.

title: Network meta-analysis: psychotherapy, pharmacotherapy and combination in adult depression
fact: A network meta-analysis of 101 trials (11,910 adults) found combined treatment most likely to produce response, about 27% more likely than psychotherapy alone and 25% more than medication alone. Psychotherapy alone and medication alone did not differ significantly in response. Most trials lasted 8 to 16 weeks, so long-term outcomes are unknown.
source: Cuijpers P, et al. A network meta-analysis of the effects of psychotherapies, pharmacotherapies and their combination in the treatment of adult depression. World Psychiatry 2020;19:92-107.
note: Confirmed via NIHR Evidence summary (https://evidence.nihr.ac.uk/alert/combined-drug-and-psychological-therapies-may-be-most-effective-for-depression/); original WPS page not opened. 2020 is before the book's 2021/22 edition, so use as supporting, not new, evidence; no post-2021 combined-treatment meta-analysis was verified.

title: Short-term vs long-term MBT for BPD: randomized trial
fact: In a trial of 166 outpatients with subthreshold or diagnosed BPD, 5 months of MBT was compared with 14 months. BPD symptoms at 16 months did not differ between the groups, nor did secondary outcomes such as self-harm. Serious adverse events (mostly hospitalizations) were numerically more frequent with long-term MBT, not significantly.
source: Juul S, Jakobsen JC, Hestbaek E, et al. Short-term versus long-term mentalization-based therapy for borderline personality disorder: a randomized clinical trial (MBT-RCT). Psychother Psychosom 2023;92(5):329-339.
note: Confirmed from fetched PMC page PMC10716869 abstract. Does not test MBT against no-treatment.

title: Cochrane review of psychological therapies for BPD
fact: The review concluded that MBT appears more effective than treatment as usual for self-harm, suicidality and depression at end of treatment, and DBT also beat usual care on several outcomes. The authors rated this evidence as low quality, so the results could change with more data.
source: Storebo OJ, et al. Psychological therapies for people with borderline personality disorder. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;5(5):CD012955.
note: Confirmed via PubMed record (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32368793, fetched); authors list not shown there but attribution is Storebo et al. as in the request. Predates 2021.

title: Review of psychoeducation in bipolar disorder
fact: A literature review of 70 randomized trials (searched to April 2022) found psychoeducation associated with fewer relapses, mood episodes and hospitalizations and with better functioning and quality of life. Some studies also reported better medication adherence and less self-stigma. Online and mindfulness-based formats were called promising but needing more evidence.
source: Levrat V, Favre S, Richard-Lepouriel H. Current practices of psychoeducation interventions with persons with bipolar disorders: a literature review. Front Psychiatry 2023;14:1320654 (published Jan 2024).
note: Confirmed from Frontiers page (fetched). It is a narrative literature review, not a meta-analysis. A 2022 group CBT/psychoeducation meta-analysis (PMC9691241) appeared in search but its page was blocked, so not used.

title: Narrative therapy for depressive symptoms in adults with somatic disorders
fact: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 54 randomized trials (4,879 participants) found a large reduction in depressive symptoms with narrative therapy in people with physical illness (SMD -1.64). The evidence was rated low quality, most trials were from China, and only 2 studies involved patients with a depression diagnosis.
source: Hu G, Han B, Gains H, Jia Y. Effectiveness of narrative therapy for depressive symptoms in adults with somatic disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Int J Clin Health Psychol 2024;24(4):100520.
note: Confirmed from Elsevier journal page (fetched). Body text reportedly grades evidence very low and publication bias tests were significant; treat the large effect cautiously. Other hits (a 2023 Frontiers meta-analysis of narrative exposure for PTSD) are narrative exposure, not narrative therapy proper.
